title: A Bounce and a Bottom Look Identical on Day One
summary: Stocks trade below their long-term average valuation, but much of that discount depends on ambitious earnings forecasts actually coming true.
body_markdown:
*Stocks trade below their long-term average valuation, but much of that discount depends on ambitious earnings forecasts actually coming true.*


***KEY TAKEAWAYS***


-


The S&P 500 has fallen 11.6% from its October record, officially entering correction territory after seven consecutive losing sessions. The Nasdaq lost 10% in a single week and is now negative for the year.


-


Stocks appear cheaper at roughly 17 times expected earnings, below their five and ten-year averages. But the lower valuation largely reflects rising earnings forecasts, not collapsing stock prices.


-


The morning rebound may be driven by short covering, portfolio rebalancing, oversold conditions, and mechanical buying by leveraged funds. Those forces can create a powerful rally without confirming a lasting bottom.


-


History suggests caution after a seven-day losing streak. Corrections that avoid becoming bear markets have historically been deeper and longer than the current decline, although averages never dictate an exact outcome.


-


Investors should watch market participation, earnings expectations, and leverage to judge whether the rally is sustainable. Today’s price action alone cannot answer that question.


***MY HOT TAKES***


-


Relief rallies are emotional catnip. A green screen after a brutal selloff can feel like confirmation even when absolutely nothing has been fixed.


-


Stocks are only “cheap” if Wall Street’s earnings forecasts come true. A low P/E built on heroic profit assumptions is not a bargain–it is a bet.


-


Leverage is the passenger nobody wants to discuss. Borrowed money makes rallies look stronger on the way up and turns ordinary selling into a stampede on the way down.


-


Buying a correction can be smart, but buying the first bounce blindly is not bravery. Taking three seconds to inspect the car is discipline, not bearishness.


-


The index price is the least interesting part of this rally. Participation, earnings, and leverage will determine whether this is a durable bottom or simply another open door on the way down.


-


You can quote me: “ *Relief is a feeling. It is not a signal.”*


***Why is this car empty?*** Every New Yorker learns it exactly once. The train (we call the subway ‘The Train’ in New York, FYI) pulls in–packed, every car, faces pressed against the glass–and then there it is. ONE car. Empty. Seats for everybody. The doors open like a gift. The tourist steps in smiling. The New Yorker stops, sniffs, and walks briskly to the next car to stand shoulder-to-shoulder with eighty strangers. Why? Because in this town an empty car on a crowded train is NEVER good luck. It is empty for a reason–busted air conditioning in August if you are lucky, something far worse if you are not. 🤣 I learned that one the hard way on the Lex (that’s my fav train line) many years ago. This morning, after seven straight days of selling, the market pulled into the station with a wide-open car and futures up by almost 3% while I was writing this. Looks inviting. Hold that thought.


You know what happened last week, so I will be quick. The S&P 500 fell 3.70% on Friday, its SEVENTH straight loss–the longest losing streak since February of 2020, and I don’t have to remind you what was going on in February of 2020. The Nasdaq Composite dropped 5.28% on the day and 10% on the week, its worst week since that same pandemic spring, and it is now in the red for the year. The Dow gave up 950 points to close at 48,147. Add it all up and the S&P sits 11.6% below the record it set on October 6. That is a correction (a decline of 10% or more from a high, for those keeping score). Wall Street’s so-called fear gauge, the VIX, finished the week near 36, its highest close since the tariff panic of April 2025. And this morning? Green. The stocks that got hit hardest on Friday are leading the way back. Seats for everybody.


And I am not gonna lie–it is a nice-looking car. The S&P 500 now trades at roughly 17 times the earnings Wall Street expects over the next twelve months (that is the forward P/E in Wall Street talk). The five-year average is 19.8. The ten-year average is 19.1. This index started the year at 22, and that 17 was hit before Friday’s drop, so the tag is probably a touch lower still. When was the last time you could say that stocks were CHEAPER than their own ten-year average? It has been a while. But here is the part that gets lost. A P/E has two letters, and most of the markdown came from the ‘E’, not the ‘P.’ Stocks did not get cheap this year because prices collapsed–they got cheap because earnings estimates climbed faster than prices did. The Street is penciling in profit growth of better than 28% for the current quarter. That’s right, twenty-eight percent! So the seat is only a bargain if those earnings actually show up. Q3 results beat estimates by about 3%, which is less than half the usual cushion. Keep that in your back pocket.


Now, why are the doors open this morning? Not because anything got fixed over the weekend. Nothing did. Markets bounce after a week like that for reasons that have very little to do with conviction. Traders who bet against stocks have to buy in order to take their profits–yes, that is short covering. Funds that must hold a fixed mix of stocks and bonds find themselves light on stocks and have to top up. And the tape was simply stretched. By Friday’s close, only about one in five S&P 500 stocks was still trading above its average price of the past twenty days, and the index itself was some 6% below its 200-day average. On three separate days last week, roughly 80% of the volume on the New York Stock Exchange was in falling stocks. Pull a rubber band that far and it WILL snap back. That tells you plenty about the rubber band. It tells you nothing about who was pulling. I have watched more of these mornings than I care to count, and the first green open after a rout always feels the same. Like relief. But let me be clear here, my friends. *Relief is a feeling. It is not a signal.*


So I dusted off the record books. Since 1950, one month after the S&P 500 has fallen seven days in a row, it was higher just 48% of the time. On any ordinary day, that number is 62%. In other words–a coin flip, and a slightly bent one. Now, to be fair, six months out the odds improve to about three in four. Here is another. There have been 25 corrections since 1946 that stopped short of becoming bear markets–the GOOD kind, if there is such a thing. On average, they took the market down 14.1% and needed 130 days to find a bottom. We are down 11.6% and it has only been 45 days. Does that mean there is more to go? No. Averages are not appointments. But it does mean that a correction which ended last Friday would be shallower and a LOT quicker than the typical one. I lived through a market in the early 2000s that served up one convincing rally after another on its way down the stairs. Every single one of them had seats available.


This brings me to who is already riding in that car. Borrowed money. According to FINRA, investors owed their brokers $1.45 trillion in margin loans at the end of October. That was down a bit from the summer’s record but still the fourth-highest reading ever. The Federal Reserve’s own stability report, published ten days ago, found hedge fund leverage at its highest level since it began keeping track in 2013. Now, those numbers are stale, and I want to be straight with you about that. They tell us how much borrowed money walked INTO last week. They do not tell us how much was carried out. That is precisely the problem–nobody knows yet. What I can tell you is what the dip-buyers were reaching for. Last Thursday, as investors pulled $11.65 billion out of the oldest and most heavily traded S&P 500 fund in a single day, nearly half a billion dollars went INTO a fund built to deliver three times the daily move of the Nasdaq 100. A similar triple-strength fund tied to chip stocks lost about 47% of its value last week. 👀 Those funds have a quirk, by the way. To keep their promise, they must sell when the market falls and buy when it rises–automatically, every afternoon, no judgment involved. They are buyers this morning. Guess what they are on the next bad day. That’s right. 🤕


One more thing about this train. In most of the corrections I have lived through, there was a conductor willing to hold the doors–a Federal Reserve that could cut interest rates if things got ugly. Not this time. Futures markets put the chance of a rate HIKE on December 9 at about nine in ten, and the yield on the 10-year Treasury is a touch under 5% even after last week’s scramble for safety. The Fed’s preferred inflation gauge–PCE Price Index–lands Wednesday at 8:30 Wall Street Time, the day before the market closes for Thanksgiving, when half of Wall Street will be at the airport. Thin crowds. Big number. What could go wrong? 🤣


Here is why all of this matters to you as an investor. A bounce and a bottom look IDENTICAL on day one. What separates them shows up later, and it shows up in three places. Participation–whether hundreds of stocks join the rally or just the same handful that fell the hardest. Earnings–whether that 28% holds up when companies start talking about next year, beginning with two big sellers of AI hardware that report in the next two days. And borrowed money–whether the next margin figure shows that the leverage actually left. None of that is likely to be known by lunch today. And notice that not one of the three is a price. The price is the open door. Everything that matters is inside the car.


I am not telling you the car is a trap. Sometimes–not often, but sometimes–an empty car is just an empty car, and the fellow who hesitated stands for forty blocks feeling foolish. Stocks ARE cheaper than they were six weeks ago, and corrections do end. But I have been riding these trains a long time, and I have never once regretted the three seconds it takes to look through the window first. Check the seats. Check the floor. Check whether the other passengers paid their own way, or whether they are riding on borrowed money. Then, by all means, step in and sit down. Just breathe through your mouth until 14th Street. 🤣


***FRIDAY’S MARKETS***


*Stocks tumbled on Friday as the S&P 500 fell for a seventh straight session and closed in correction territory, with Nvidia sinking 14.01% after reports surfaced that SEC staff are examining the company's accounting. The S&P 500 dropped 3.70%, the Nasdaq Composite lost 5.28%, the Russell 2000 slid 2.76%, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1.93%, or 950 points to 48,147. The 10-year Treasury yield fell about 12 basis points to roughly 4.92% and the 2-year dropped about 13 basis points to 4.63% as investors moved into government bonds. WTI crude settled up $0.77 at $83.98 and Brent rose $0.59 to $92.57, while the VIX closed near 36, its highest finish since April 2025.*


***NEXT UP***


-


S&P Global US Manufacturing PMI (November) is expected to have slipped to 54.5 from 54.9.


-


S&P Global US Services PMI (November) may have declined to 55.5 from 56.1.


-


Later this week: remember that Thursday is closed for Thanksgiving and Friday has an early close. Despite the abridged week, we will still get some important earnings along with some more housing numbers, Consumer Confidence, Personal Income, Personal Spending, GDP, PCE Price Index, and Durable Goods Orders.


-


Important earnings today: ***Crowdstrike, Zscaler, Agilent, Fluence Energy, HP Enterprise,*** and ***Zoom Communications.***
